subject: Geography
unit: Unit One: Major Geological Processes Associated with Plate Tectonics

slides.title: Continental Drift Theory
content: • Theory proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912.
• Suggests that the Earth's continents have moved over geologic time.
• Presents the idea of a supercontinent called Pangaea that existed around 350 million years ago.
• During the Triassic period, Pangaea split into two large landmasses: Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south).
• These larger landmasses later fragmented into the present-day continents.

slides.title: Geological Evidences Favoring Continental Drift Theory
content: • Coastline Similarity: The coastlines of Africa and South America fit together like a jigsaw puzzle.
• Rock type and structural similarities: When continents are fitted together, similar rock types of the same age are found across them.
• Fossil Evidence: Identical fossils of Mesosaurus found on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean.
• Paleoclimatic Evidence: Ancient climatic data, reconstructed from rocks, show similarities across continents.

slides.title: Why Wegener's Theory was Rejected
content: • Wegener was not a geologist by profession.
• Most influential scientists at the time were in the Northern Hemisphere, but much of the conclusive data came from the Southern Hemisphere.
• The perceived timeframe for such massive continental drift was considered too short.
• There was no plausible explanation for the mechanism driving the movement of continents.

slides.title: Legacy of Wegener's Theory
content: • Introduced the idea of lateral mobility of continents.
• Shifted scientific thinking from 'fixism' to 'mobilism'.
• Ignited a new way of viewing the Earth and inspired further research.
• Paved the way for the development of the Plate Tectonics Theory.

slides.title: Plate Tectonics Theory
content: • Developed in the late 1960s, it explains how the Earth's outer layers move and deform.
• States that the Earth's lithosphere (crust and uppermost mantle) is broken into about a dozen large plates.
• Plates move on the asthenosphere, a ductile layer below.
• Plates can be composed of continental, oceanic, or both types of crust.
• The theory is universally accepted and has revolutionized the field of geology.

slides.title: Key Concepts of Plate Tectonics
content: • Lithosphere: The rigid outer layer of the Earth, consisting of the crust and uppermost mantle.
• Asthenosphere: The ductile, partially molten layer of the mantle below the lithosphere, allowing plates to move.
• Plate Boundaries: The edges where plates interact, responsible for most geological activity.
• Convection Currents: The movement of heat in the mantle (hot material rises, cools, and sinks) that drives plate motion.

slides.title: Significance of Plate Tectonics
content: • Provides a framework for understanding major geological features:
- Mountains, earthquakes, volcanoes.
- Distribution of fossils and rock ages.
• Influences the composition of the atmosphere and oceans.
• Serves as a prime cause of long-term climate change.
• Explains almost all aspects of what we see on the Earth's surface.

slides.title: Types of Plate Boundaries
content: • Convergent (Destructive) Boundaries: Plates move toward each other.
- Subduction of one plate under another.
- Forms volcanoes, mountain ranges, and volcanic islands.
• Divergent (Constructive) Boundaries: Plates move apart.
- Upwelling magma creates new crust.
- Forms seafloor spreading, oceanic ridges, and rift valleys.
• Transform (Conservative) Boundaries: Plates slide past each other laterally.
- Crust is neither created nor destroyed.
- Associated with major faults and earthquakes.

slides.title: Convergent Plate Boundaries
content: • Oceanic-Continental Convergence: Denser oceanic plate subducts under the continental plate.
- Example: The Andes Mountains (Nazca Plate under South American Plate).
• Oceanic-Oceanic Convergence: One oceanic plate subducts under another.
- Example: Mariana Islands.
• Continental-Continental Convergence: Two continental plates collide and buckle.
- Example: The Himalayas (Indo-Australian Plate with Eurasian Plate).

slides.title: Divergent and Transform Boundaries
content: • Divergent Boundaries:
- Process of seafloor spreading.
- Forms undersea mountain chains (oceanic ridges).
- Can create rift valleys on continents (e.g., East African Rift Valley).
• Transform Boundaries:
- Plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes.
- Example: The San Andreas Fault in California.
• The motion is driven by convection currents in the mantle.

slides.title: Internal (Endogenic) Forces
content: • Forces that originate from inside the Earth and create irregularities on the surface.
• Key processes include:
- Folding: Rock layers bend due to compression, forming anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds).
- Faulting: Rocks break and displace along fractures, creating rift valleys and block mountains.
- Earthquakes: Sudden shaking caused by the release of energy along faults.
- Volcanism: Magma rises to the surface through vents, building volcanoes and plateaus.

slides.title: Folding and Faulting
content: • Folding:
- Young fold mountains: Andes, Rockies, Himalayas (formed in recent Alpine orogeny).
- Old fold mountains: Appalachian, Urals (older, more weathered).
• Faulting:
- Rift Valleys: Land sinks between two faults (e.g., East African Rift Valley).
- Block Mountains (Horsts): Land is pushed up between two faults (e.g., Afar Horst).

slides.title: Earthquakes
content: • Sudden shaking of the ground due to the shifting of rock masses along faults.
• Focus: The point where the rock ruptures underground.
• Epicenter: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
• Seismic Waves: Shock waves that travel through the Earth (P and S waves).
• Effects: Ground movement, landslides, fires, and tsunamis.
• Occur mostly along plate boundaries, like the Pacific Ring of Fire.

slides.title: Volcanism and Volcanoes
content: • Volcanism: The process by which magma reaches the surface.
• Volcanoes can be active, dormant, or extinct.
• Types of Volcanoes:
- Shield Volcanoes: Broad and flat (e.g., Hawaiian Islands).
- Strato Volcanoes: Steep cones with alternating layers of lava and ash (most common).
- Cinder Cone Volcanoes: Small, conical hills made of pyroclastic material.
• Other features: Craters, calderas, and intrusive landforms like sills and dikes.

slides.title: External (Exogenic) Forces
content: • Forces that act on the Earth's surface from the outside.
• They level the landscape through denudation and deposition.
• Denudation includes:
- Weathering: The breakdown of rocks (physical and chemical).
- Erosion: The movement of weathered material (by water, wind, sea waves, glaciers).
• Examples: Exfoliation (thermal expansion), Frost action, Stalactites and Stalagmites (chemical).

slides.title: Erosion and Deposition
content: • Running Water: Erodes to form V-shaped valleys, gorges, waterfalls, and deltas.
• Wind: Forms sand dunes, barkhans, and loess deposits.
• Sea Waves: Forms beaches, spits, and lagoons.
• Mass Wasting: The downslope movement of rock and soil under the influence of gravity.
• These processes shape the present-day land surface and create a variety of landforms.

slides.title: Understanding Climate Change
content: • Climate change refers to a change in the state of the climate that persists for an extended period (decades or longer).
• It can be identified by changes in the mean and/or variability of its properties.
• It is caused by both natural processes and human activities.
• Often associated with global warming, but its consequences are much broader.

slides.title: Global Warming and its Impacts
content: • Global warming is the long-term heating of Earth's surface.
• It is primarily caused by human activities (burning fossil fuels).
• Consequences include: stronger hurricanes, melting glaciers, loss of wildlife habitats, and rising sea levels.
• The Earth's air, water, and land are interdependent, so a change in one area leads to changes in others.

slides.title: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
content: • The leading international body for assessing the science related to climate change.
• Provides comprehensive reports on the state of climate change.
• Reports show that climate change is happening across the planet, largely due to human activities.
• Evidence comes from observations of the atmosphere, land, and oceans.
• Important Greenhouse Gases: Carbon Dioxide (CO2), Methane (CH4), and Nitrous Oxide (N2O).

slides.title: Observed Climate Trends
content: • The Earth's climate has always changed, but recent changes are being driven by human activities.
• Activities: Deforestation, industrial emissions, and transport.
• These activities release greenhouse gases (GHGs) that trap heat and warm the planet.

slides.title: IPCC Assessment Reports
content: • The IPCC's 2001 Report documented that the 1990s were the warmest decade since instrumental records began (1861).
• The 20th century was likely the warmest in the last 1,000 years.
• Most of the warming over the past 50 years has resulted from human activities.
• The average global surface temperature has warmed by 0.80°C in the past century.

slides.title: Future Projections
content: • If GHG emissions continue to rise, mean global temperatures will increase by 1.4°C to 5.8°C by the end of the 21st century.
• Impacts on Sea Level: Rise in sea levels due to melting ice and thermal expansion.
• Changes in Snow Cover and Rainfall: Shifts in regional climate patterns.
• These changes are already affecting watersheds and ecosystems in many parts of the world.

sections.section: 2.3. Natural and Human Induced Climate Change

slides.title: Natural Causes of Climate Change
content: • Natural phenomena have caused climate change in the past.
• External causes include:
- Changes in incoming solar radiation.
- Changes in the composition of the atmosphere.
- Changes in the Earth's surface.
• Internal causes: Changes in ocean and atmosphere circulation patterns.
• Examples: Milankovitch cycles (changes in Earth's orbit), variations in solar output (sunspots), and volcanic eruptions.

slides.title: Human (Anthropogenic) Induced Climate Change
content: • The dominant cause of warming since the mid-20th century is human activity.
• Activities include: burning fossil fuels (emitting GHGs) and land-use changes (deforestation).
• Humans are also injecting aerosols and particles into the atmosphere.
• The IPCC's 2013 Report states it is 'extremely likely' (95% probability) that human influence is the dominant cause.

slides.title: The Enhanced Greenhouse Effect
content: • The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life on Earth.
• However, human activities are increasing the concentration of GHGs (CO2, CH4, N2O).
• This 'enhanced' greenhouse effect traps too much heat, causing global warming.
• Deforestation reduces the Earth's capacity to absorb CO2.

slides.title: Impacts on Climate and Weather Patterns
content: • Land areas are warming more rapidly than the global average, especially in high northern latitudes.
• Changes in precipitation: Some areas get more intense rainfall, while others experience severe droughts.
• The frequency and intensity of extreme weather events are increasing.
• Impacts on Agriculture: Food security is threatened due to unpredictable weather patterns.

slides.title: Rising Sea Levels and Polar Regions
content: • Sea level rise is caused by thermal expansion of seawater and melting of land-based ice.
• Globally, sea levels rose about 19 cm from 1900 to 2010 and the pace is accelerating.
• In the Polar Regions:
- Arctic sea ice is shrinking dramatically.
- Ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica are melting.
- This has severe impacts on wildlife and weather patterns.

slides.title: Effects on Ecosystems and Human Well-being
content: • Increasing CO2 acts as a 'fertilizer' for some plants, but can cause others to become dominant.
• Many species are forced to migrate to cooler areas or face extinction.
• Human Health: Increased heatwaves, spread of diseases (e.g., malaria), and food insecurity.
• The impacts are interconnected: climate change affects species distributions and human well-being.

sections.section: 2.5. Adaptation and Mitigation Strategies to Climate Change

slides.title: Mitigation: Addressing the Cause
content: • Mitigation aims to limit climate change by reducing GHG emissions.
• It involves reducing the sources of GHGs (burning fossil fuels) and enhancing sinks (forests).
• Examples: Transitioning to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, and planting trees.

slides.title: Adaptation: Managing the Impacts
content: • Adaptation aims to alleviate the adverse impacts of climate change.
• It involves adjustments in ecological, social, or economic systems.
• Types of Adaptation:
- Reactive: After impacts occur.
- Anticipatory: Before impacts become apparent.
- Planned: Deliberate policy decisions.
- Autonomous: Natural responses to change.
• Examples: Soil conservation, water harvesting, crop diversification, and planting trees.

sections.section: 2.6. International conventions and agreements on climate

slides.title: Key Milestones in Climate Agreements
content: • 1979: First World Climate Conference identifies climate change as a global problem.
• 1988: Toronto Conference recommends a global framework convention.
• 1990: The IPCC publishes its First Assessment Report.
• 1992: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) is adopted.

slides.title: The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement
content: • Kyoto Protocol (1997): Set mandatory emission reduction targets for developed countries.
- The US did not ratify it, and developing countries were not required to reduce emissions.
• Paris Agreement (2015): Adopted by virtually all nations.
- Under the agreement, each nation sets voluntary targets for reducing emissions.
- It represents a shift to a more flexible, bottom-up approach.

slides.title: Pathways to Combating Climate Change
content: • The most obvious way to limit global warming is to reduce the use of fossil fuels.
• Transition to renewable energy sources: solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal.
• Creating a worldwide culture of sustainable development is essential.
• This includes using energy efficiently and promoting eco-friendly products.

sections.section: 2.7. Pillars of Climate Resilient Green Economy of Ethiopia

slides.title: Introduction to Ethiopia's CRGE Strategy
content: • Ethiopia aims to follow a green growth path that fosters development and sustainability.
• The Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategy focuses on four pillars.
• The goal is to achieve middle-income status by 2025 while reducing GHG emissions.

slides.title: Pillar I: Agriculture
content: • Improving crop and livestock production practices.
• Goal: Increase farmer income and food security while reducing emissions.
• Priorities include limiting soil-based emissions and reducing pressure on forests.
• Increasing resource efficiency and productivity in the livestock sector.

slides.title: Pillar II: Forests
content: • Protecting and re-establishing forests for their economic and ecosystem services.
• Goal: Reverse deforestation and forest degradation.
• Prioritizes reducing demand for fuelwood and increasing afforestation.
• Promotes area closure to increase carbon storage in Ethiopian forests.

slides.title: Pillars III & IV: Energy and Industry
content: • Pillar III: Expanding electricity generation from renewable sources.
- Exploiting potential for hydro, geothermal, solar, and wind power.
- Clean energy also enables green development in other sectors.
• Pillar IV: Leapfrogging to modern and energy-efficient technologies.
- Focus on transport, industrial sectors, and buildings.
- Promoting fuel efficiency, electric rail networks, and alternative fuels.

subject: Geography
unit: Unit Three: Issues in Sustainable Development I: Management of Conflict over Resources

slides.title: Historical Overview of Sustainable Development
content: • 1972: First UNCED in Stockholm introduced 'eco-development' and created UNEP.
• 1987: Second UNCED in Nairobi introduced the idea of 'sustainable development'.
• 1987: Brundtland Commission defined it as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'.
• 1992: Earth Summit in Rio developed 'Agenda 21'.
• 2002: World Summit in Johannesburg emphasized social and economic aspects.

slides.title: The Three Pillars of Sustainable Development
content: • Economic: An economically sustainable system must produce goods and services on a continuing basis.
- Maintain manageable levels of government and external debt.
• Environmental: An environmentally sustainable system must maintain a stable resource base.
- Avoid overexploitation of non-renewable resources, maintain biodiversity.
• Social: A socially sustainable system must achieve fairness in distribution and opportunity.
- Provide adequate social services such as health, education, and gender equity.

slides.title: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
content: • Adopted by the United Nations in 2015 as a universal call to action.
• 17 goals, integrated and recognize that action in one area affects outcomes in others.
• Aims to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure peace and prosperity by 2030.
• Examples: No Poverty (1), Zero Hunger (2), Climate Action (13).
• Integrated into Ethiopia's development plans (GTP II and CRGE strategy).

slides.title: Criticisms of Sustainable Development
content: • Incorrectness of the term and its internal logical contradiction.
• Narrowness of the term, often confining global problems to the environmental context.
• Implementation difficulties due to multiple concept definitions.
• Criticism that the concept only benefits a certain part of humanity.
• Despite criticisms, the transition to a sustainable path requires a dramatic transformation.

sections.section: 3.2. Resource Use Policies and Related Conflicts

slides.title: Types of Resources and Conflict Drivers
content: • Renewable Resources: Can replenish themselves (e.g., water, forests).
• Non-renewable Resources: Finite and cannot be replaced (e.g., minerals, fossil fuels).
• Resource Conflicts are often over:
- Ownership, access, decision-making, and distribution of benefits.

slides.title: Main Drivers of Conflict over Natural Resources
content: 1. Competition over increasingly scarce renewable resources.
- Demand-induced scarcity, supply-induced scarcity, structural scarcity.
2. Poor governance of renewable natural resources.
- Unclear rights, discriminatory policies, unequal distribution, lack of transparency.
3. Transboundary natural resource dynamics.
- Shared water resources, wildlife migration, and pollution crossing borders.

slides.title: Case Study: The Nile Basin
content: • Transboundary water management is a key diplomatic issue for the 11 Nile Basin countries.
• Upstream countries (e.g., Ethiopia) argue for an equitable allocation of water resources.
• The Nile Basin Initiative (NBI) was established in 1999 to coordinate management.
• Debates center on the construction of dams and the right to water for irrigation and power.

slides.title: Conflict Prevention and Sustainable Livelihoods
content: • Conflict prevention involves approaches to avoid, minimize, and resolve conflict.
• The Sustainable Livelihoods Framework helps reduce vulnerability to resource scarcity.
• Strategies include livelihood diversification, efficiency improvements, and adaptation.
• Approaches aim to protect livelihoods and prevent the erosion of assets.

slides.title: What is Natural Resource Governance?
content: • Refers to the norms, institutions, and processes that determine power over natural resources.
• How decisions are taken and how citizens, including indigenous peoples, participate.
• Good governance is essential for preventing conflict and ensuring sustainable development.

slides.title: Principles of Good Natural Resource Governance
content: 1. Legal and institutional changes to clarify resource rights and responsibilities.
2. Equitable resource access should be a priority of public policy.
3. Transparent environmental and social impact assessments for all projects.
4. Increased public participation and transparency in decision-making.
5. Adaptability to unexpected impacts on renewable resources.

slides.title: Governance and Indigenous Rights
content: • Indigenous communities are particularly affected by natural resource exploitation.
• International conventions like the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) recognize their rights.
• Consultation, access to information, and access to justice are vital for protecting their rights.
• The Aarhus Convention advances public participation in environmental matters.

slides.title: Introduction to Indigenous Conflict Resolution
content: • Societies worldwide have used indigenous mechanisms to prevent and resolve conflicts.
• These mechanisms are often based on community customs, familial relationships, and institutional practices.
• In Ethiopia, they are deeply rooted in the culture and traditions of different ethnic groups.
• They are often preferred due to lack of access to justice and the high cost of formal legal systems.

slides.title: Examples of Indigenous Institutions in Ethiopia
content: • Oromo: Gadaa system, including Gumma for cases of unintentional killing.
• Amhara: Shimagle (council of elders).
• Somali: T'eer (customary law) and guurti (council of elders).
• Afar: Mada'a (led by elders, based on customary law).

slides.title: Effectiveness of Indigenous Systems
content: • They are more accessible and less costly than formal courts.
• They prioritize reconciliation and peaceful coexistence.
• They lead to 'win-win' outcomes by considering the interest of every party.
• They avoid the 'zero-sum' outcomes of the formal legal system.
• However, they are often seen as an alternative to the formal system, not a replacement.

slides.title: UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP)
content: • Adopted in 2007, it makes direct reference to indigenous peoples' rights to land and self-determination.
• Article 7: Recognizes the right to live in freedom, peace, and security.
• Article 32: Recognizes the right to determine development priorities for their lands.
• Article 40: Recognizes the right to access just procedures for resolving conflicts.

subject: Geography
unit: Unit Four: Issues in Sustainable Development II: Population Policies, Programs and the Environment

sections.section: 4.1. Theories on Population Growth and Development

slides.title: Malthusian Theory
content: • Proposed by Thomas Malthus (1798).
• Population grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8...).
• Food production grows arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4...).
• Leads to a 'Malthusian Crisis' where population outstrips food supply.
• Checks on Population:
- Positive Checks: Famine, disease, and war (increase death rate).
- Preventive Checks: 'Moral restraint' (late marriage, celibacy).

slides.title: Neo-Malthusianism
content: • Follows Malthus's idea that population growth is a main cause of poverty.
• Unlike Malthus, they see birth control as the solution.
• Advocate for family planning and contraceptive use.
• View rapid population growth as a cause of:
- Poverty, environmental destruction, unemployment, and political instability.
• Critics argue it diverts attention from social and economic causes of poverty.

slides.title: Radical Theories: Boserup and Simon
content: • Ester Boserup's Hypothesis:
- Population growth stimulates innovation and agricultural development.
- 'Necessity is the mother of invention.'
• Julian Simon's 'Ultimate Resource' Theory:
- People are the ultimate resource.
- Human ingenuity can solve resource problems.

slides.title: The Marxian Perspective
content: • Karl Marx's View:
- Poverty is not caused by overpopulation.
- It is caused by unequal distribution of resources.
- In capitalism, the owning class controls the means of production, creating poverty.
• Critics of Malthusian/Neo-Malthusian theories:
- They are ethnocentric.
- They ignore the unequal distribution of global resources.

slides.title: Definition and Types of Population Policies
content: • Population Policy: A policy formulated by a government to plan and control population growth, based on economic, social, and demographic conditions.
• Two Main Categories:
- Pro-natalist Policy: Aims to increase fertility rates. (e.g., France, Sweden).
- Anti-natalist Policy: Aims to lower fertility rates. (e.g., China's one-child policy).

slides.title: Pro-Natalist Policies
content: • Seek to encourage higher birth rates.
• Implemented in countries with low fertility rates and aging populations.
• Policy measures include:
- Financial incentives (family allowances, tax breaks).
- Maternity/paternity leave.
- Childcare subsidies.
- Housing subsidies.

slides.title: Anti-Natalist Policies
content: • Seek to reduce birth rates.
• Common in countries facing rapid population growth and resource strain.
• Policy measures include:
- Family planning programs.
- Access to contraceptives.
- Health and education services for women.
• Most well-known example: China's One-Child Policy.

sections.section: 4.3. Measures Taken to Curb Growth of Population

slides.title: Methods of Population Control
content: • Child Tax: Higher taxes for parents with more children.
• One-Child Policy: Restrict family size to one child.
• Family Planning: Access to safe, voluntary means of planning a family.
- This is considered a human right and is central to gender equality.

slides.title: International Conferences and Global Context
content: • Bucharest Conference (1974): Introduced the World Population Plan of Action.
• Cairo Conference (1994): Shifted focus from 'numbers' to women's empowerment.
- Recognized the link between population growth and development.
• Today, most developing countries have national population policies and subsidize family planning.

slides.title: Examples from Various Cultures
content: • China: Implemented one-child policy (1979-2015).
• India: Focuses on women's education and empowerment.
• Africa: Birth rates are the highest; many countries have active family-planning campaigns.

slides.title: Challenges of Population Control
content: • Obstacles to implementing policies:
- Lack of availability and accessibility of services.
- Cultural and religious opposition.
- Language barriers.
- Lack of awareness.
- Wife/husband acceptance.

slides.title: The Concept of Development
content: • Development is a process by which members of a society increase their capacities to mobilize and manage resources.
• It aims for sustainable improvements in quality of life.
• Key objectives:
- Increase the availability and distribution of basic life-sustaining goods.
- Raise living standards and levels of income.
- Expand the range of economic and social choices.

slides.title: Measures and Indicators of Development
content: • GDP/GNP: Measures the value of goods and services produced.
• Per-Capita Income: National income divided by population size.
• Standard of Living: Level of income, comforts, and services available.
• Countries are classified as developed, less developed, and least developed.
• Social Indicators: Literacy rates, life expectancy, infant mortality.

slides.title: Factors of Economic Development
content: • Economic Factors:
- Natural Resources, Capital Expenditure, Technology.
• Non-Economic Factors:
- Labor Force (human capital), Social Values, Political Stability.

slides.title: Social Implications of Population Growth
content: • Rapid population growth is linked to many problems.
- Poverty, hunger, high infant mortality.
- Inadequate social services and infrastructure.
• It can reduce or eliminate food production gains.
• It increases the absolute numbers whose needs must be met.
• Problems are compounded when people migrate to cities.

sections.section: 4.5. Relationship Between Population and Environmental Health

slides.title: What is Environmental Health?
content: • Environmental health comprises aspects of human health that are determined by factors in the environment.
• This includes physical, biological, social, and psychosocial factors.
• The UN Agenda 21 (1992) addresses health issues, with a focus on primary healthcare, communicable diseases, and reducing health risks from pollution.

slides.title: Environmental Health Intervention Models
content: 1. Clinical Model: Treating disease after it has occurred.
2. Public Health Model: Controlling disease-causing agents.
3. Environmental Stewardship Model: Proactively addressing environmental problems.

slides.title: Key Environmental Health Issues
content: • Air pollution is the world's largest single environmental risk to health.
• Unsafe water and poor sanitation cause major mortality in low-income countries.
• Degraded ecosystems lead to food insecurity and disease outbreaks.
• Zoonotic diseases (e.g., COVID-19, Ebola) are emerging more frequently.
• An integrated approach linking environment and health is essential.

subject: Geography
unit: Unit Five: Issues in Sustainable Development III: Challenges of Economic Development

sections.section: 5.1. Multiple Faces of Poverty and Implication to Development

slides.title: Concepts of Poverty
content: • Poverty is a measure of deficiency of basic needs.
• Absolute Poverty: Household income is below a certain level, making it impossible to meet basic needs (food, shelter, water).
• Relative Poverty: Households receive 50% less than average incomes. They are not in absolute poverty but cannot afford the standard of living others in the society enjoy.

slides.title: Causes of Poverty
content: • Structural Approach: Points to systemic reasons for poverty.
- Racial and gender discrimination, low wages, and failure to invest in education and healthcare.
• Behavioral/Cultural Approach: Emphasizes culture, behavior, and personal differences.
- A 'poverty culture' with attitudes that perpetuate self-defeating decisions.

slides.title: Relationship between Conflict and Poverty
content: 1. Conflict causes poverty: Destruction and displacement lead to long-term economic costs.
2. Poverty causes conflict: Grievances and resource competition can fuel violence.
3. Resource wealth causes conflict: The prospect of exploiting resources can fuel rebellion.

sections.section: 5.2. The Advantages and Disadvantage of Globalization

slides.title: What is Globalization?
content: • The process by which the world becomes more linked through greater commerce, political integration, and cultural interaction.
• It has accelerated dramatically in the last half-century.
• It is driven by multinational corporations and global mass media.

slides.title: Impacts on Developing Countries
content: • Economic: Opens markets, creates jobs, but can also lead to exploitation and pollution.
• Education and Health: Improves access to knowledge and technology, but can lead to 'brain drain'.
• Culture: Spreads ideas and ideals but can erode local traditions and languages.

slides.title: Advantages of Globalization
content: • Increased free trade between nations.
• Increased liquidity of capital.
• Global mass media ties the world together.
• Reduction of cultural barriers.
• Spread of democratic ideals.
• Reduction of the likelihood of war between developed nations.

slides.title: Disadvantages of Globalization
content: • Decreased environmental integrity.
• Exploitation of cheap labor.
• Threat to cultural diversity.
• Increased risk of disease transmission.
• Spread of a materialistic lifestyle.
• Increased chances of civil war as countries vie for resources.

sections.section: 5.3. The Growing Imbalance between Regions and Countries

slides.title: Economic Inequality
content: • The idea of inequality is both simple and complex.
• Convergence Hypothesis: Less developed countries should grow faster than more developed ones.
• Divergence Reality: The gap between rich and poor is widening.

slides.title: Trade Imbalance
content: • A trade imbalance occurs when the cost of imports exceeds the cost of exports.
• Causes: When a country doesn't produce what it needs and borrows to pay for imports.
• Effects: Can enhance standard of living but may result in job outsourcing.

slides.title: Measuring Inequality: The Gini Coefficient
content: • A measure of income or wealth distribution.
• Ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).
• Sub-Saharan Africa has some of the highest levels of inequality in the world.

slides.title: The Widening Global Imbalance
content: • Inequality has increased in most developed countries since 1990.
• In developing countries, it has remained stable but at a much higher level.
• Inequality is exacerbated by technological development and the collapse of labor institutions.

slides.title: What is Corruption?
content: • The abuse of entrusted power for private gain.
• It is a political, economic, legal, and moral phenomenon.
• Causes: Weak institutions, lack of transparency, and poor governance.

slides.title: Types of Corruption
content: • Bribery: Payments to influence administrative decisions.
• Theft of Public Assets: Embezzlement and diversion of public funds.
• Patronage (Favoritism): Preferential treatment of friends and associates.
• Petty vs. Grand Corruption: Based on the scale of the transaction.

slides.title: The Geography of Corruption
content: • Measured by Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index (CPI).
• Scores range from 0 (most corrupt) to 100 (least corrupt).
• Most corrupt countries are low-income, have closed economies, and low media freedom.
• Least corrupt countries are typically wealthy democracies with strong institutions.

slides.title: Consequences and Remedial Measures
content: • Consequences:
- Distorts public investment.
- Reduces the effectiveness of public spending on health and education.
- Undermines tax revenues.
• Remedial Measures:
- Strong leadership with integrity.
- A responsible press.
- Independent oversight bodies.
- Institutional reforms (legal framework, police, judiciary).

slides.title: Global Health Challenges
content: • An estimated 2 billion people lack access to basic health services.
• Low- and middle-income countries bear 90% of the global disease burden but receive only 12% of global health spending.
• Health crises expose the vulnerability of poor governance and weak health infrastructure.

slides.title: Historical Pandemics
content: • The Great Plague of Athens (430 BC) was one of the first recorded pandemics.
• The 1918 'Spanish Flu' was the most famous pandemic, killing 50 million people.

slides.title: Contemporary Health Crises
content: • HIV/AIDS: First identified in 1981, has caused 35 million deaths.
• Ebola (2013-2016): Devastated West Africa, revealing weak public health infrastructure.
• COVID-19 (2019-present): Spread globally at an unprecedented pace, affecting all nations.

subject: Geography
unit: Unit Six: Issues in Sustainable Development IV: Solutions to Environmental and Sustainability Problems

slides.title: Major Global Environmental Problems
content: • Environmental problems are now global in existence and impact.
• The environmental formula: I = f(P, A, T)
- I = Environmental Impact.
- P = Population.
- A = Affluence/Consumption.
- T = Technology.

slides.title: Climate Change and Ozone Depletion
content: • Climate Change: The most discussed environmental problem with observable ecological and social effects.
• Ozone Layer Depletion: Caused by CFCs; the Montreal Protocol successfully reduced these chemicals.

slides.title: Biodiversity Loss and Pollution
content: • Biodiversity Loss: Natural ecosystem degradation and species extinction continue rapidly.
• Air Pollution: Includes primary pollutants (CO, NO2, SO2) and secondary pollutants (smog).
• Water Pollution: Contaminants from agriculture, industry, and urban areas degrade water quality, creating ocean 'dead zones'.

slides.title: Land Degradation
content: • Land Degradation: A negative trend in land condition, caused by human-induced processes.
• 24 billion tons of fertile soil are lost per year.
• Soil Contamination: The presence of harmful substances in soil, often from leaks or pollution.
• The Global Environmental Facility (GEF) works on sustainable land management.

slides.title: Challenges to Sustainability
content: • The impact of climate change threatens to escalate.
• Hunger and malnourishment remain persistent.
• Income inequality has reached extremely high levels.
• Rapid urbanization calls for major changes in urban design.
• Energy needs remain unmet for hundreds of millions.

slides.title: Core Sustainability Challenges
content: • Population Growth: Projected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, straining resources.
• Urbanization: 60% of the world's population will live in cities by 2030.
• Energy Use: Burning fossil fuels is the primary driver of global warming.
• Water Scarcity: A country is water-scarce if it has less than 1,000 m³ of renewable freshwater per capita.
• Waste Management: The world generates 2.01 billion tons of municipal solid waste annually.

slides.title: Sustainable Solutions
content: • Combating Climate Change: Through renewable energy and preserving ecosystems.
• Renewable Energy: Solar chimney, wind farm, hydropower, and geothermal.
• Green Buildings: Designed to minimize natural resource consumption and emissions.
• Role of Soil Microorganisms: To increase yields in an environmentally acceptable manner.

slides.title: What is Environmental Education?
content: • Education 'in, about, and for' the environment.
• Aims to develop an ecologically literate population that is motivated to take action.
• It is a lifelong, interdisciplinary process.

slides.title: Goals and Types of Environmental Education
content: • Goals:
- Foster awareness of environmental interdependence.
- Provide knowledge, values, and skills.
- Create new patterns of behavior.
• Formal vs. Informal Education.
• The continuum of education includes: Information, communication, education, and capacity-building activities.

slides.title: Fundamental Characteristics of Environmental Education
content: • Lifelong Learning: Involves everyone, from youth to adults.
• Interdisciplinary: Links natural sciences, social sciences, and humanities.
• A Proven Strategy: Links knowledge with action.
• Focus on Critical Thinking: Teaches people how to think, not what to think.

slides.title: What is an Environmental Movement?
content: • A social movement involving an array of individuals, groups, and coalitions.
• They perceive a common interest in environmental protection.
• Their goal is to bring about changes in environmental policies and practices.

slides.title: Types of Environmental Movements
content: • Free Market Environmentalism: Uses property rights and markets.
• Preservation vs. Conservation: Strict protection vs. sustainable use.
• Popular Environmentalism: Focused on 'green consumerism'.
• Light Greens: Environmentalism as a lifestyle choice.
• Dark Greens: Seek radical political change.
• Bright Greens: Advocate for change through new technologies and social innovations.

slides.title: Environmental Movements in Ethiopia
content: • Activism is rarely seen in a well-organized way.
• Notable Organizations: Lem Ethiopia.
• Individual Activists: Artist Sileshi Demise (municipal waste control).
• Leadership: Late PM Meles Zenawi (climate negotiations), PM Abiy Ahmed (Green Legacy campaign).
• The role of youth is increasingly important.

slides.title: What is Indigenous Knowledge?
content: • Unique, traditional, local knowledge developed by indigenous people.
• It is local, orally transmitted, based on practical experience.
• It is shared and embedded in broader cultural traditions.
• Application areas: ecosystem management, water management, soil conservation, and pest control.

slides.title: Examples in Ethiopia
content: • Illuababora (Oromo): Knowledge of folk medicine and conservation of medicinal plants.
• Konso: Dry stone terraces for soil conservation and water management.
• Gedeo: Traditional regulations ('seera') that protect sacred trees and the ecosystem.
• Gumuz (Western lowlands): Shifting cultivation and belief system that considers resources sacred.

slides.title: The Role of Indigenous Knowledge
content: • Indigenous practices offer effective, sustainable solutions.
• They are crucial for maintaining ecosystems and livelihoods.
• Recognizing and integrating IK into modern conservation is essential.
• These practices show that local communities are active agents of conservation.

subject: Geography
unit: Unit Seven: Contemporary Global Geographic Issues and Concerns

slides.title: Climate Change as a Global Issue
content: • Climate change is one of the most pressing contemporary global issues.
• It threatens the lives and livelihoods of billions of people.
• The Paris Agreement (2015) is a key international effort to curb emissions.
• A changing climate requires comprehensive strategies addressing social, economic, and environmental consequences.

slides.title: Predicted Impacts of Temperature Increase
content: • Health: A 2.3°C rise could put 270 million people at risk of malaria.
• Ecosystems: A 1-2°C rise could cause 15-20% of global ecosystems to change.
• Agriculture: A 2.5°C rise could put 50 million more people at risk of hunger.
• Water Resources: A 2-2.5°C rise could put 2.4-3.1 billion people at risk of water shortage.

slides.title: Observable Effects
content: • Ice is melting worldwide, especially at the poles.
• Global sea levels are rising at a faster rate.
• Wildlife and their habitats are being affected.
• Precipitation patterns are changing, causing more severe droughts in some areas and more intense rainfall in others.
• Pests and diseases are thriving.

slides.title: What is Desertification?
content: • Land degradation in arid, semi-arid, and dry sub-humid areas.
• Caused by human activities and climatic change.
• Not the same as the expansion of natural deserts.
• Drylands cover 46.2% of the global land area and are home to 3 billion people.

slides.title: Causes of Desertification
content: • Population Growth: Increased demand for food and resources.
• Over-exploitation: Over-cultivation, overgrazing, deforestation.
• Climate Change: Increased drought frequency and severity.
• Poor Irrigation Practices: Can lead to salinization.

slides.title: Consequences of Desertification
content: • Decreased land productivity.
• Food shortages and hunger.
• Increased poverty.
• Destruction of habitats and biodiversity loss.
• Forced migration.

slides.title: Desertification in Eastern Africa
content: • East Africa has large tracts of drylands highly vulnerable to desertification.
• Rapid population growth and widespread deforestation are key factors.
• National efforts: Ethiopia's 'Green Legacy' campaign.
• International efforts: UNESCO's Integrated Project on Arid Lands.

slides.title: Definition and Types of Drought
content: • Drought: A temporary reduction in water availability below normal levels.
• Types:
- Meteorological: A reduction in rainfall.
- Hydrological: A reduction in surface and groundwater.
- Agricultural: A shortage of water for agriculture (soil moisture deficit).

slides.title: Drought-Prone Regions and Indices
content: • Drought-prone regions are found in the world's dryland belts, including the Sahara, the Horn of Africa, and the Arabian Desert.
• Indices to quantify drought: Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI), Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI).
• The SPI is widely used because it can be calculated for different time scales.

slides.title: Causes and Impacts of Drought
content: • Natural Causes: El Niño/La Niña, shifts in the ITCZ.
• Human-Induced Causes: Land-use change, greenhouse gas emissions.
• Impacts: Reduced farm income, food price increases, malnutrition, migration, water shortages, and conflict.

slides.title: What is Famine?
content: • Famine is a process, not a single identifiable event.
• It results from a sequence of events that reduce food availability or food entitlements.
• This leads to widespread and substantially increased morbidity and mortality.
• It is distinct from chronic hunger.

slides.title: Causes of Famine
content: • Decline in Food Availability:
- Natural: Drought, floods, crop disease, pest invasions.
- Human-Induced: Conflict, external economic shocks, poor government policies.
• Decline in People's Ability to Acquire Food:
- Economic factors, forced procurement of farm produce.

slides.title: Measures to Maintain Food Security
content: • Price stabilization.
• Food subsidies.
• Employment creation programs.
• General food distributions.
• Supplementary feeding programs.
• Complementary water and health programs.
• These measures are essential to protect people's access to food.

subject: Geography
unit: Unit Eight: Geographical Enquiry and Map Making

slides.title: Purpose and Features of Geographic Research
content: • Research: A systematic and objective inquiry into a problem.
• Purpose of Research:
- Exploration, Explanation, Description, Understanding, Prediction.
• Features: Focus on spatial distributions, patterns, interactions, and the forces behind them.

slides.title: Research Approaches
content: • Quantitative Approach:
- Uses numerical data and statistical analysis (deductive).
- Tests theories (e.g., measuring temperature changes by altitude).
• Qualitative Approach:
- Uses descriptive data (interviews, observations).
- Generates theories (inductive).
• Mixed Methods: Combines both quantitative and qualitative techniques.

slides.title: Research Method vs. Methodology
content: • Research Method: The specific techniques for collecting data (e.g., surveys, interviews).
• Research Methodology: The philosophy and logic behind the research, justifying why certain methods are chosen.
• A research design is the overall plan for how the study will be conducted.

slides.title: Basic Elements of a Research Project
content: 1. Problem Identification and Statement.
2. Objectives (General and Specific).
3. Research Questions.
4. Research Design.
5. Determining the Sample (Probability vs. Non-probability).
6. Literature Review.
7. Data Collection (Primary and Secondary).
8. Data Analysis and Interpretation.
9. Results, Discussion, Conclusions, and Recommendations.

sections.section: 8.2. GIS Data and Map Making Using GIS

slides.title: Introduction to GIS
content: • GIS (Geographic Information System): A computer system for capturing, storing, analyzing, and presenting spatial data.
• Five fundamental components: Data, Software, Hardware, People, and Methods.
• Spatial Data: Data linked to a specific location.

slides.title: Gathering Data for GIS
content: • Data Generalization: Selecting the level of measurement:
- Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio.
• Data Dimensionality:
- Point, Line, Area (Polygon), Volume.
• Data Representation: Methods like Natural Break (Jenk's), Equal Interval, Quantile, and Standard Deviation affect map interpretation.

slides.title: GIS Data Analysis
content: • Querying:
- Attribute Query: Selecting data based on attributes.
- Spatial Query: Selecting data based on location.
• Analysis to Generate New Data:
- Proximity Analysis (Buffering): Creating zones around features.
- Overlay Analysis (Vector and Raster): Combining layers to find spatial relationships.
- Network Analysis: Finding optimal routes (e.g., for transportation).
